title: AI-Native Firms, Built by Private Equity, Will Strain Legacy Model
author: Eric Dodson Greenberg

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s premises that associate-heavy routine work is increasingly automatable and that complex judgment depends on experience and context. However, it does not establish the cluster’s central causal claim that automating junior work threatens expertise reproduction, nor does it recommend simulation, mentorship or independent practice as a response.
qs: This “judgment legal” work—governance advice, complex negotiations, high-stakes litigation, regulatory strategy where the law is fundamentally unclear—resists systematization and depends on deep contextual synthesis.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: Greenberg accepts the cluster’s core distinction between legal-AI tools and AI-enabled service providers, then materially extends it by arguing that external capital and ABS regimes can create AI-native law firms that capture repeatable work from traditional firms. He also develops the cluster’s billing-and-leverage thesis by identifying partnership incentives to retain AI gains as margin rather than pass them through as lower prices.
qs: AI-native law firms will follow this model: establish a technology platform, build client relationships as a vendor, develop service delivery capabilities, then create a regulatory-compliant law firm that competes for work that otherwise would go to traditional firms.

But the default incentive within partnership economics will be to use AI to increase profits at existing price points, not to decouple “prestige” from “price” and sell the commodity work at a discount.

st.t: AI investment: Delivery businesses may capture more value
st.an: Greenberg accepts the importance of AI-enabled legal delivery businesses and materially extends the cluster by proposing a repeatable external-capital pathway: build a technology platform and client base, develop delivery capabilities, then form a compliant law firm competing directly with incumbents. His claims support the delivery-side thesis but remain predictive rather than evidence of superior realised economics.
qs: The straightest path to AI law firms isn’t innovation within the legacy model, or capital investing around it, but external capital being deployed to build competitors to legacy firms.

AI-native law firms will follow this model: establish a technology platform, build client relationships as a vendor, develop service delivery capabilities, then create a regulatory-compliant law firm that competes for work that otherwise would go to traditional firms.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claim that in-house AI capabilities can strengthen buyers by making institutional knowledge portable and supporting unbundled purchasing. It materially extends that proposition by identifying externally financed, ABS-enabled AI-native law firms as new providers able to exploit this shift and challenge traditional partnerships, although this competitive outcome is primarily a strategic prediction rather than measured evidence.
qs: As in-house teams build their own AI capabilities, the institutional knowledge that once locked clients to specific firms becomes portable.
The straightest path to AI law firms isn’t innovation within the legacy model, or capital investing around it, but external capital being deployed to build competitors to legacy firms.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Greenberg accepts that AI will structurally reorganise legal delivery and materially extends the synthesis by specifying a vendor-to-law-firm pathway through outside capital and ABS regulation. He also strengthens the buyer-side reallocation thesis by arguing that in-house AI makes institutional knowledge portable, though his claims remain forecasts rather than evidence of market-wide change.
qs: AI-native law firms will follow this model: establish a technology platform, build client relationships as a vendor, develop service delivery capabilities, then create a regulatory-compliant law firm that competes for work that otherwise would go to traditional firms.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Greenberg accepts the cluster’s core claim that automation threatens the associate-heavy profit model while leaving judgment-intensive work intact. He materially extends it by arguing that buyer unbundling, portable in-house knowledge, external capital and AI-native law firms could turn task efficiency into direct structural competition, especially because partnership incentives discourage incumbents from rebuilding delivery models.
qs: Singular expertise is packaged with large teams of associates doing industrial analytical work at scale.
As in-house teams build their own AI capabilities, the institutional knowledge that once locked clients to specific firms becomes portable.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: Greenberg accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI adoption is a business-model and competitive-structure problem, then materially extends it by specifying how external capital, ABS openings and AI-native firms could bypass partnership incentives, unbundle profitable routine work and shift client knowledge ownership toward corporate legal departments. These are principally argued mechanisms and predictions, not demonstrated market-wide outcomes.
qs: The straightest path to AI law firms isn’t innovation within the legacy model, or capital investing around it, but external capital being deployed to build competitors to legacy firms.

But the default incentive within partnership economics will be to use AI to increase profits at existing price points, not to decouple “prestige” from “price” and sell the commodity work at a discount.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Greenberg accepts the cluster’s core view that AI can reconfigure legal-service delivery and shift work and bargaining power toward legal departments and AI-native providers. He materially extends it by identifying external capital and ABS openings as mechanisms for building integrated competitors outside incumbent partnerships, while explaining how buyer-side unbundling and client-owned knowledge systems may erode firms’ bundled economics and knowledge advantage. These are strategic predictions rather than evidence of completed market-wide displacement.
qs: The straightest path to AI law firms isn’t innovation within the legacy model, or capital investing around it, but external capital being deployed to build competitors to legacy firms.
As in-house teams build their own AI capabilities, the institutional knowledge that once locked clients to specific firms becomes portable.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Greenberg reinforces the cluster’s claim that organisational structure and market adaptation—not AI access alone—govern value. He materially extends it by arguing that incumbent firms’ investment constraints, buyer-side unbundling and external capital for AI-native providers could erode firms’ knowledge advantage and reshape provider competition, while treating the outcome as contingent rather than established.
qs: This leaves traditional firms at a structural disadvantage against new competitors.

External capital is knocking on the door at some traditional firms—both Quinn Emanuel and McDermott Will & Schulte have signaled openness to outside investment—but its biggest impact is funding the entirely new AI-native model.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Greenberg accepts that AI primarily disrupts labour-intensive legal production while context-dependent judgment remains valuable. He materially extends the cluster by proposing a specific competitive mechanism: externally funded, AI-native law firms using ABS openings, client-owned institutional knowledge and technology-enabled delivery to challenge incumbent partnership economics directly. His market-wide forecast is more assertive than the cluster’s cautious assessment, but it remains aligned with restructuring rather than autonomous replacement of lawyers.
qs: This “judgment legal” work—governance advice, complex negotiations, high-stakes litigation, regulatory strategy where the law is fundamentally unclear—resists systematization and depends on deep contextual synthesis.
The straightest path to AI law firms isn’t innovation within the legacy model, or capital investing around it, but external capital being deployed to build competitors to legacy firms.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: Greenberg accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI-enabled delivery will shift value capture across firms, platforms and clients, and materially extends it with a specific competitive mechanism: outside capital can build AI-native law firms that bypass partnership constraints, capture automatable volume work and weaken incumbent client dependence through client-owned knowledge systems. His argument is primarily a strategic forecast supported by entrant examples, not evidence of market-wide outcomes.
qs: The straightest path to AI law firms isn’t innovation within the legacy model, or capital investing around it, but external capital being deployed to build competitors to legacy firms.
And crucially, it belongs to—and resides with—the client, not the firm.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-selective account: repeatable industrial work is increasingly automatable, while contextual judgment remains resistant to systematisation. It materially extends the synthesis by explaining how that division threatens Big Law’s bundled profit model, enabling AI-native platforms to capture industrial workflows without reproducing elite relationship-led expertise.
qs: Tech-first platforms may not offer the blockbuster name, but they’re designed to capture the popcorn sales.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: Greenberg accepts the cluster’s core claim that corporate buyers increasingly unbundle work and that AI-enabled delivery can pressure legacy firms. He materially extends it by identifying external capital and Arizona’s ABS framework as a concrete route for building AI-native competitors with integrated workflows, pricing and service delivery. His account is more disruption-oriented than the synthesis and does not address its junior-training and verification concerns.

kp.k: Capital is building AI-native competitors to legacy firms
kp.d: Greenberg argues that the legal market is developing a “third way” beyond technology adoption by incumbent firms and investment in adjacent vendors or providers: external capital is financing new, AI-native law firms designed from inception around integrated technology, workflows, service delivery, and pricing. This is primarily a strategic argument and prediction about market structure rather than an empirical finding.
qs: But this false binary misses an emergent third way.
The straightest path to AI law firms isn’t innovation within the legacy model, or capital investing around it, but external capital being deployed to build competitors to legacy firms.
These firms use AI and narrow regulatory openings to create from scratch tech-enabled law firms.
Not acquire them. Not invest around them.
Build them.

kp.k: Norm Law exemplifies the emerging AI-native model
kp.d: As evidence that the model is already emerging, the article reports that former Sidley Austin executive committee chair Mike Schmidtberger became chairman of Norm Law in January 2026. Norm Law is described as a recently formed AI-native legal platform backed by Bain Capital, Blackstone, and Vanguard; Schmidtberger characterizes his move as encountering a fundamentally different technological future.
qs: At the end of 2025, Mike Schmidtberger left Sidley Austin, one of the nation’s leading and largest law firms, after chairing its executive committee for seven years.
The next month, he became chairman of another law firm: Norm Law—a two-month-old AI-native legal platform backed by Bain Capital, Blackstone, and Vanguard.
When he walked through the doors of Norm Law, he told Bloomberg Law he “confronted the future.”

kp.k: Regulatory openings enable externally funded law firms
kp.d: Greenberg identifies Arizona’s Alternative Business Structure regime, which permits non-lawyer ownership, as the regulatory opening enabling technology businesses and externally backed providers to establish law firms. He cites Eudia Counsel, KPMG, and LegalZoom as examples. He discloses that he sits on Eudia’s Client Advisory Board, qualifying his discussion of that company.
qs: Arizona’s Alternative Business Structure framework—allowing non-lawyer ownership of law firms—opened regulatory space that didn’t previously exist.
Eudia (on whose Client Advisory Board I sit) established Eudia Counsel last fall, an ABS-licensed law firm combining the capabilities of AI and alternative legal service providers.
KPMG opened a US law practice under ABS rules.
LegalZoom and others followed similar paths.

kp.k: Vendor platforms may evolve into competing law firms
kp.d: The article predicts a staged entry strategy for AI-native providers: first establish technology and vendor relationships, then build service-delivery capacity, and finally create a compliant law firm. Such entrants would move beyond selling software or supporting incumbent firms to compete directly for legal work.
qs: AI-native law firms will follow this model: establish a technology platform, build client relationships as a vendor, develop service delivery capabilities, then create a regulatory-compliant law firm that competes for work that otherwise would go to traditional firms.
They represent a new strategic paradigm—one that sidesteps both the cultural resistance of established partnerships and the circuitous investment models that try to work around them.

kp.k: AI, capital, and reform create mutually reinforcing change
kp.d: Greenberg’s central causal argument is that AI-enabled restructuring of legal work, external financing, and regulatory reform reinforce one another rather than operating independently. He predicts that their convergence will accelerate competitive pressure from new entrants.
qs: When forces like these converge—AI restructuring how legal work gets done, external capital funding those positioned to leverage it, and legal regulatory reform creating an opening for new entrants—they don’t add.
They multiply.

kp.k: Legal work is splitting into industrial and judgment segments
kp.d: The author divides legal services into “industrial legal” work—high-volume, repeatable, process-dense tasks such as document review, due diligence, scaled contracting, and compliance monitoring—and “judgment legal” work involving ambiguity, relationships, creativity, and contextual synthesis. He asserts that industrial work is increasingly automatable, while judgment-intensive work resists systematization.
qs: One segment—“industrial legal”—is process-dense, labor-intensive, high-volume, and offers substantial margins: document review, due diligence, contracting at scale, compliance monitoring.
This work is analytical, repeatable—and increasingly automatable.

This “judgment legal” work—governance advice, complex negotiations, high-stakes litigation, regulatory strategy where the law is fundamentally unclear—resists systematization and depends on deep contextual synthesis.

kp.k: Traditional profitability bundles expertise with leveraged industrial work
kp.d: Greenberg argues that large firms derive substantial profit by bundling prestigious partner judgment with associate teams performing scalable industrial work. Using a movie-theater analogy, he predicts that technology-first platforms will target the repeatable work that supplies much of the margin, even if they lack prominent individual lawyers.
qs: Traditional firms make their greatest profits not necessarily from the star partners of the judgment practice, but from bundling both segments.
Singular expertise is packaged with large teams of associates doing industrial analytical work at scale.
The star sells tickets, but the theater makes its money on popcorn.
Tech-first platforms may not offer the blockbuster name, but they’re designed to capture the popcorn sales.
And in legal services, industrial work is the popcorn—and the profit.

kp.k: Partnership incentives discourage passing AI savings to clients
kp.d: The article reports a theory that Big Law could combine elite expertise with AI efficiency, but Greenberg argues that partnership incentives favor using AI to preserve prices and increase margins rather than reducing prices for commoditized work. He identifies profits per partner and associate leverage as continuing performance measures that support this tendency.
qs: One theory posits that Big Law will bridge this divide by synthesizing deep expertise with AI efficiency.

But the default incentive within partnership economics will be to use AI to increase profits at existing price points, not to decouple “prestige” from “price” and sell the commodity work at a discount.
The cultural and governance structure of large partnerships tilts toward margin preservation, with profits-per-partner and associate leverage still treated as primary scorecards.

kp.k: AI platforms could make institutional knowledge a compounding asset
kp.d: Greenberg contrasts lawyer-dependent institutional memory with technology-first systems that purportedly retain approaches, reasoning, tradeoffs, and client-specific logic across matters. He argues that this knowledge can compound independently of individual lawyers and, where it resides with the client, reduce dependence on specific outside counsel relationships. These are asserted capabilities and strategic implications, not measured outcomes.
qs: In the tech-first platform, every contract, negotiation, and filing feeds a system that captures not just what was done, but how it was approached—the reasoning, the tradeoffs, the institutional logic.
That knowledge compounds independently of any individual lawyer.
And crucially, it belongs to—and resides with—the client, not the firm.
The GC who owns the institutional memory—rather than renting it from a firm—has a structural advantage that traditional outside counsel relationships no longer match.

kp.k: In-house AI may reduce inconsistency and attrition risks
kp.d: For general counsel and expanding legal departments, the author argues that centralized AI-enabled knowledge could standardize documents, strategy, and risk approaches while preserving organizational practices when personnel change. An unnamed fellow general counsel is quoted as framing human inconsistency across a large department as a risk alongside AI’s own risks.
qs: AI-enabled centralization of knowledge mitigates the risks of a legacy model in which in-house teams produce inconsistent documents, deploy differing strategies, or adopt varied risk profiles.
As a fellow GC put it to me directly: “AI has its risks—but so does having a hundred lawyers each doing things their own way.”
AI-enabled knowledge systems hedge both inconsistency and attrition: New talent can be coached by AI on “how we do things here” rather than learning through trial and error.

kp.k: The article claims AI-retained knowledge is more durable
kp.d: Greenberg asserts that individual lawyer knowledge degrades or departs with personnel, whereas AI-retained knowledge can remain accessible and current. The claim supports his broader argument that clients can own portable institutional memory, but the article supplies no study, sample, or comparative performance evidence establishing this durability or currency.
qs: Lawyer knowledge is fundamentally not shelf-stable—memories fade, contexts shift, people leave.
AI-retained knowledge is stable, current, and always available.

kp.k: Annual profit distribution impedes long-term technology investment
kp.d: The author describes a “partnership trap” in which annual cash distributions, lateral talent competition, and profits-per-partner rankings discourage investments whose benefits accrue to future partners or clients. He presents this governance structure as a structural disadvantage relative to externally funded AI-native competitors able to invest for longer-term capability building.
qs: The emphasis that law firms place on annual cash distributions is in perennial tension with long-term capability building.
Every dollar invested in infrastructure benefits future partners and clients at the cost of current partners’ cash.
In an active lateral market, those yearly distributions become essential to talent retention.
When those distributions are expressed as profits-per-partner, they drive the rankings that determine a firm’s prestige and viability.
Near-term cash is what holds partnerships together.

kp.k: Client unbundling and portable knowledge weaken firm lock-in
kp.d: Greenberg states that corporate legal departments increasingly allocate different matter types to specialized providers rather than relying on a single full-service firm. He predicts that in-house AI capabilities will make institutional knowledge more portable, weakening the knowledge-based client lock-in that historically favored incumbent firms and aligning purchasing behavior with technology-first platforms.
qs: Corporate legal departments increasingly unbundle work.
Rather than routing work to an all-purpose firm, they frequently match matter type to provider specialty—such as sending IP matters to a specialized boutique.
As in-house teams build their own AI capabilities, the institutional knowledge that once locked clients to specific firms becomes portable.
Tech-first platforms align with how legal consumers are already behaving.

kp.k: External capital may breach traditional firms’ knowledge moat
kp.d: The article concludes that although some traditional firms have signaled openness to outside investment, external capital’s larger effect may be to finance entirely new AI-native providers. Greenberg predicts that the combination of capital, technology, and portable knowledge will erode incumbent firms’ longstanding competitive protection, while leaving the ultimate market outcome contingent on their response.
qs: External capital is knocking on the door at some traditional firms—both Quinn Emanuel and McDermott Will & Schulte have signaled openness to outside investment—but its biggest impact is funding the entirely new AI-native model.
Law firms have long been protected by a knowledge moat.
The convergence of capital and tech is beginning to breach it.
How traditional firms respond will shape what’s on the other side.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Greenberg predicts that external capital will build AI-native law firms that compete directly with traditional firms, rather than merely financing technology around them.
pts.d: The author describes a third route beyond traditional firms adopting AI and investors funding adjacent businesses: building new firms with AI embedded in delivery, pricing, and workflow. He predicts a progression from technology platform to vendor relationships, service delivery capabilities, and a regulatory-compliant law firm. He argues that the combination of AI, capital, and regulatory openings has a multiplicative competitive effect. Schmidtberger's description of encountering the future is presented as his personal assessment of joining Norm Law, not as demonstrated market impact.

pts.k: Greenberg argues that AI-native providers threaten the profitable, repeatable work traditionally bundled with high-end legal judgment.
pts.d: He distinguishes 'industrial legal' work—document review, due diligence, large-scale contracting, and compliance monitoring—from relationship-dependent, ambiguous 'judgment legal' work. He claims the former is increasingly automatable and supplies substantial profits through associate-heavy delivery, whereas the latter resists systematization. Tech-first competitors are positioned to capture industrial work without supplying the traditional firm's prestige offering. He acknowledges a theory that Big Law can combine expertise and AI efficiency, but predicts that partnership incentives will favor maintaining prices and margins rather than discounting commodity work.

pts.k: Greenberg claims that AI-native systems turn institutional legal knowledge into a compounding, client-held asset independent of individual lawyers.
pts.d: He contrasts traditional files, which he says preserve outcomes rather than the judgment behind them, with platforms that capture reasoning, tradeoffs, and institutional logic from legal work. He argues that this makes knowledge available despite departures, reduces reliance on particular outside partners, and gives general counsel a structural advantage. His characterization of AI-retained knowledge as stable, current, and always available is an asserted capability; the article does not present a measured implementation result or explain updating requirements.

pts.k: Greenberg claims AI-centralized knowledge reduces in-house inconsistency and attrition risks and supports onboarding.
pts.d: For expanding corporate legal departments, he argues that shared knowledge systems mitigate differences in documents, strategies, and risk profiles and can coach new employees in the organization's established practices. An unnamed fellow general counsel supplies a supporting risk comparison, acknowledging AI risks while emphasizing the risks of inconsistent human practice.

pts.k: Greenberg argues that partnership economics constrain long-term investment while client unbundling and AI-enabled knowledge portability weaken traditional firms' competitive protection.
pts.d: He links annual partner distributions, lateral retention pressures, profits-per-partner rankings, and associate leverage to incentives that preserve the legacy model. Meanwhile, he says corporate buyers increasingly allocate work by provider specialty and develop their own AI capabilities, making knowledge formerly tied to outside firms portable. He predicts that outside capital's largest effect will be financing new AI-native competitors, notwithstanding some incumbent firms' openness to investment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The emergence claim is supported with named firms, regulatory examples, an executive move, and adjacent legal-technology investment activity.
pts.d: Greenberg reports that Schmidtberger left Sidley Austin at the end of 2025 and became chairman of Norm Law the next month, describing Norm as a two-month-old AI-native platform backed by Bain Capital, Blackstone, and Vanguard. He identifies Arizona's ABS framework as enabling nonlawyer ownership and cites Eudia Counsel, KPMG's US law practice, and LegalZoom as examples. He also cites Harvey's $300 million raise at a $3 billion valuation, Fastcase and Brightflag consolidation, and Anthropic's legal plugin as context for technology investment and disruption—not as measured evidence of AI-native firms taking incumbent revenue. He discloses membership on Eudia's Client Advisory Board.

pts.k: Claims about profitability, knowledge systems, investment incentives, and buyer behavior rest chiefly on qualitative argument and practitioner perspective.
pts.d: The author is Cox Media Group's executive vice president, general counsel, and corporate secretary. He supplies a structural account of partnership incentives, a movie-theater analogy for bundled profitability, observations about corporate procurement, and an unnamed GC's comment about inconsistency. The article offers no task benchmarks, quantified automation savings, segment-level margin data, client-retention measurements, or longitudinal evidence of knowledge-system performance. Its predictions about market displacement and the largest future use of outside capital are arguments rather than reported quantitative findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article frames the transition as already beginning in late 2025–March 2026, with further competitive effects predicted but no deadline.
pts.d: Published March 23, 2026, the article anchors emergence in Schmidtberger's end-2025 departure and January 2026 appointment and Eudia Counsel's establishment 'last fall.' Future expansion depends on external financing, regulatory-compliant entry through limited openings, developed delivery capabilities, and client relationships. Automation exposure is qualified by work type: repeatable industrial tasks are increasingly automatable, while contextual judgment work resists systematization. Knowledge portability is linked to in-house AI development. The author does not specify when displacement will occur, how large it will be, or that all legal work will unbundle; further unbundling is explicitly left for the series' second part.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are incumbent corporate law firms, AI-native entrants and investors, corporate legal buyers, and lawyers whose work or client relationships underpin the legacy model.
pts.d: Traditional firms face competition for high-volume work, pressure on bundled profits, and weaker dependence on individual partners' knowledge. Associates are implicated through the industrial work and leverage supporting those profits, but the article gives no explicit headcount or job-loss forecast. Judgment-focused partners remain differentiated by experience, creativity, relationships, and contextual synthesis. AI-native firms and external investors gain a route into direct legal-service delivery; KPMG is cited as a Big Four entrant under ABS rules, distinct from software vendors such as Harvey. General counsel and in-house teams are described as gaining institutional memory, consistency, onboarding support, and provider flexibility. The discussion concerns predominantly corporate legal services, not individual access to justice.
